blocks.text: Chemical shift gives the position of a signal relative to a reference compound. Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH3)4 (TMS), is the standard reference, and its signal is given the value 0.0 ppm; all other signals are measured from it. The position of a peak in a 1H NMR spectrum relative to the TMS peak is the chemical shift (delta), measured in parts per million (ppm). The chemical shift shows the electronic environment of a proton: protons in different environments have different delta values, and those in the same environment have the same value.

blocks.title: Did you know? Why TMS?
blocks.text: All 12 protons of TMS have the same environment, so it gives one sharp peak. Silicon has a low electronegativity, so the TMS peak lies at the far right of the spectrum and does not overlap most organic signals. TMS is also chemically inert and volatile, so it is easy to remove afterwards.
In the 1H NMR spectrum of methanol, the methyl (-CH3) hydrogens appear at 3.35 ppm and the O-H hydrogen at 4.80 ppm, measured from TMS at 0.0 ppm.

blocks.alt: Left: tetramethylsilane, a silicon atom bonded to four CH3 groups; all 12 H are equivalent, giving one sharp peak set at 0.0 ppm. Right: a sketch of the 1H NMR spectrum of methanol from 6 to 0 ppm, with lines at 4.80 ppm (O-H), 3.35 ppm (CH3) and 0.0 ppm (TMS).
blocks.caption: TMS and the 1H NMR spectrum of methanol (original diagram after the book's TMS box and Figure 30.2).
blocks.long_description: The scale runs from right to left: 0.0 ppm at the TMS peak on the right, and larger delta values to the left. The O-H proton of methanol, next to electronegative oxygen, appears further to the left than the CH3 protons.

blocks.text: Protons in a molecule are surrounded by electrons, and this electron density affects the NMR spectrum; protons in different parts of a molecule are in different 'environments' because of the atoms and bonds near them. All protons in chemically identical environments within a molecule are chemically equivalent and have the same chemical shift. All the protons in TMS, methane, ethane, benzene, cyclohexane and propanone are chemically equivalent, so each of these compounds gives a single peak. Molecules with sets of chemically different protons give more than one peak: propane and methanol have two environments, and 1-chloropropane and ethanol have three.

The chemical shift of a proton depends on the electron density around it. Protons surrounded by high electron density (alkyl groups) have lower chemical shifts, while protons in low electron density, near electronegative atoms such as F, O, N or Cl, appear at higher chemical shifts. In methanol the CH3 protons appear at 3.35 ppm, with more electron density around them, while the O-H proton, next to electronegative oxygen, appears at 4.80 ppm. A 1H NMR spectrum covers 0-12 ppm.

Bottom: horizontal bars on a 13 to 0 ppm scale for the shift ranges of RCOOH, RCHO, Ar-H, C=CH, Ar-OH, CH next to O or Cl, CH next to Ar, CH next to C=O, R-OH and alkyl CH; low electron density (deshielded) to the left, high (shielded) to the right.
blocks.caption: Counting proton environments and typical chemical shifts (original diagram after the book's examples and Table 30.1).
blocks.long_description: Each set of equivalent protons gives one signal, so counting environments predicts the number of peaks. Electron-withdrawing neighbours, such as O, Cl, C=O or an aromatic ring, move a proton's signal to the left (higher delta).

blocks.alt: A 1H NMR spectrum with the chemical shift axis running from 3 ppm on the left to 0 ppm (TMS) on the right. There is a single sharp peak near 0.2 ppm. Beside it, CH4 is labelled: all four hydrogen atoms are in the same environment, so they give one signal.
blocks.caption: 1H NMR spectrum of methane: one signal (original diagram after Figure 30.3).
blocks.long_description: All four protons of methane are chemically equivalent, so they absorb at the same chemical shift and give one peak. The peak lies close to TMS because the protons are shielded by the electrons of the carbon-hydrogen bonds.

blocks.prompt: Why do the 12 protons of TMS give only one peak?
blocks.explanation: They are all in the same chemical environment (each is in a CH3 group bonded to the same Si), so they are chemically equivalent.

blocks.prompt: How many proton environments are there, and at what shifts, in (i) propane, (ii) propan-2-ol, (iii) butan-2-one?
blocks.explanation: (i) Propane: 2 (CH3 and CH2), both alkyl, 0.5-1.5 ppm. (ii) Propan-2-ol: 3, CH3 0.5-1.5, CH next to O 3.0-4.5, OH 0.5-6.0. (iii) Butan-2-one, CH3COCH2CH3: 3, CH3 next to C=O 2.0-2.6, CH2 next to C=O 2.0-2.6, CH3 of the ethyl group 0.5-1.5.

blocks.prompt: The book also asks about '1,1,2,2-dichloroethane'. How many environments would it have?
blocks.explanation: The name is printed incorrectly. Both 1,2-dichloroethane (ClCH2CH2Cl) and 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane (Cl2CHCHCl2) have all their protons equivalent: one environment, shifted to high delta by the chlorine atoms.

blocks.prompt: What proton environment does a signal at delta 7.5 ppm most likely represent?
blocks.explanation: A hydrogen on an aromatic ring (Ar-H, 6.5-9.0 ppm).
